candidates.attacker_control: The attacker supplies the entire XML passed to XStreamer.fromXML. The document's first object is the serialized XStream configuration; the attacker can name types for its fields (e.g. a SecurityMapper permission list containing com.thoughtworks.xstream.security.AnyTypePermission) and for its converter registry (e.g. converters from the com.thoughtworks.xstream package, which the outer permission set explicitly allows). The payload object read afterwards is then processed by that attacker-defined XStream. Class attributes such as 'class="[L...;"' / java.lang.Class values further widen what the attacker can express inside that configuration, since JavaClassConverter resolves names with its own DefaultMapper (JavaClassConverter.java:74-80, DefaultMapper.java:66-85), which is outside the permission-checking chain.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that SecurityMapper.realClass is the chokepoint for element names, class/resolves-to attributes, aliases, collection items and references, and that it is applied while reading the embedded configuration (i.e. the outer instance does enforce permissions on that first read) — so the flaw is specifically that the reconstructed instance's policy, not the caller's, governs the payload. Checked XStreamer's default permission list (XStreamer.java:54-64) rather than assuming: it intentionally allows all of com.thoughtworks.xstream.**, Mapper/XStream/TypePermission hierarchies, so the embedded configuration can be fully specified by an attacker. Checked that the no-argument fromXML overloads route through the same implementation (XStreamer.java:212-214, 243-246). Checked that XStream's documented security guidance only warns against deserializing arbitrary user-supplied content in general (security.html:17-35, 68-72) and that the XStreamer javadoc does not warn that the embedded XStream configuration is attacker-controlled; the javadoc phrase 'load the contained XStream instance with default permissions' refers to the outer read and is misleading with respect to the payload read. No test harness exists in this snapshot (xstream/src/test is absent), so no runtime confirmation was possible; this remains a source-level candidate.
candidates.impact: When this API is used on untrusted data, the application's security framework (the default 1.4.10 whitelist or a custom permission set) is not enforced for the payload. An attacker can have XStream instantiate arbitrary classes present on the classpath, populate their fields, and invoke readResolve()/readObject() hooks (AbstractReflectionConverter.unmarshal path), which is the same capability classically abused for remote code execution via deserialization gadget chains, plus memory/CPU exhaustion. It is a bypass of the library's central mitigation, not merely a hardening gap.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must expose XStreamer.fromXML (or an overload) to untrusted XML, i.e. treat a 'self-contained' stream as data rather than a locally produced artifact. The reconstructed configuration must be constructible from classes allowed by the outer permission set (XStreamer.PERMISSIONS plus the default whitelist) — the set is deliberately broad for com.thoughtworks.xstream.** and for TypePermission/Mapper/XStream hierarchies, which is what makes the embedded configuration attacker-writable. Full RCE additionally requires a usable gadget on the classpath once permissions are widened; at minimum it is a security-control bypass yielding arbitrary type instantiation/readResolve invocation under the attacker's policy.
candidates.root_cause: XStreamer.fromXML(driver, Reader, TypePermission...) creates an `outer` XStream that is restricted by the caller-supplied/default permissions (XStreamer.PERMISSIONS, XStreamer.java:54-64, 261-266), reads an embedded `com.thoughtworks.xstream.XStream` instance out of the same untrusted XML (XStreamer.java:268), and then immediately uses that attacker-reconstructed instance to deserialize the rest of the document (XStreamer.java:269-273). The reconstructed instance carries attacker-chosen state including its SecurityMapper permission list and its converter registry, and the only permission check performed while reading that state is against the *outer* permission set, which by design allows XStream's own configuration types (TypeHierarchyPermission(TypePermission.class), Mapper, XStream, WildcardTypePermission on the com.thoughtworks.xstream package, XStreamer.java:54-64). Consequently the payload after the embedded configuration is deserialized under the attacker's policy, not the application's.
candidates.title: XStreamer.fromXML rebuilds an attacker-controlled XStream (permissions + converters) from the same untrusted document, defeating the type-permission whitelist
candidates.trace: XStreamer.fromXML(Reader) (XStreamer.java:212-214) -> fromXML(HierarchicalStreamDriver, Reader, TypePermission...) (XStreamer.java:259) -> `new XStream(driver)` plus caller permissions (XStreamer.java:261-264) -> `outer.createObjectInputStream(reader)` (XStreamer.java:266) -> `configIn.readObject()` returns the embedded XStream (XStreamer.java:268) -> `configured.createObjectInputStream(reader)` (XStreamer.java:269) -> `in.readObject()` (XStreamer.java:272) deserializes the payload using the attacker-reconstructed security setup. Because SecurityMapper.addPermission() lets a reconstructed instance install AnyTypePermission.ANY (SecurityMapper.java:64-69; AnyTypePermission.java:21-24), the whitelist configured by the application on the outer instance no longer constrains the payload.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no tests/execution allowed and xstream/src/test is absent from the snapshot. I did not enumerate an end-to-end gadget chain that works with only the default whitelist classes; the demonstrated effect is the permission/converter-policy bypass, with RCE contingent on classpath gadgets and on the application exposing XStreamer to untrusted input. I also could not verify how common this usage is, nor whether upstream considers XStreamer streams trusted by contract.
candidates.weakness_type: Deserialization of untrusted data / security-control bypass (whitelist bypass leading to arbitrary object instantiation)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 477 files with no exclusions (no binaries, symlinks, or oversized files skipped); the P1 relation index covers the same 477 files with zero missing files and no SAST/findings oracle loaded. I reviewed the security framework and its default whitelist (com.thoughtworks.xstream.security.*, SecurityMapper, XStream.setupSecurity/setupConverters/setupImmutableTypes), the mapper chain order (XStream.buildMapper:560-590), type resolution (HierarchicalStreams, AbstractCollectionConverter, AbstractReferenceUnmarshaller, TreeUnmarshaller), reflection/serialization converters (AbstractReflectionConverter, SerializableConverter, ExternalizableConverter, LambdaConverter, CustomObjectInputStream/OutputStream, SerializationMembers), the extended converters built on reflection/class names (JavaClass/JavaMethod/JavaField/DynamicProxy, java.time converters), the XML drivers' XXE configuration, and XStreamer. Documentation in xstream-distribution/src/content (security.html, faq.html, changes.html) was used only to establish intended behavior and known limitations. xstream-builder, xstream-hibernate, xstream-jmh and xstream-benchmark were surveyed only at file level, not audited line by line.
limitations: xstream/src/test is absent from the snapshot, so no tests or PoCs could be inspected; nothing was executed and no runtime confirmation was attempted or claimed.

The vulnerable-commit/fix-commit relationship for this snapshot could not be established from local evidence; xstream-distribution/src/content/changes.html documents releases only through 1.4.9 with an 'Upcoming 1.4.x maintenance release' section that does not yet contain a security entry, so the exact upstream advisory targeted by this case could not be confirmed without external data (no web access permitted).
xstream-builder, xstream-hibernate, xstream-jmh and xstream-benchmark sources were reviewed only at file/entry level, so a vulnerability localised there would not have been found.

Gadget-chain exploitability depends on the application's classpath, which is not part of the snapshot; the submitted candidate's impact is therefore stated as a demonstrated security-control bypass with RCE contingent on external gadgets.

The relation index is syntactic/navigation-only (no data-flow or reachability proof); every indexed hint used (e.g. XStreamer deserialization hints) was re-verified in source text, and index absence in an area was not treated as evidence that the area is clean.

rejected_leads.lead: Dynamic-proxy / EventHandler RCE (CVE-2013-7285 style) in the default configuration
rejected_leads.reason: Blocked: DynamicProxyMapper.DynamicProxy is a concrete static class (DynamicProxyMapper.java:67) not matched by InterfaceTypePermission, ProxyTypePermission is not a default permission, and ReflectionConverter refuses java.beans.EventHandler (ReflectionConverter.java:42-44). No default path recreates the classic gadget.

rejected_leads.lead: Array element/component types bypass the permission whitelist (ArrayConverter.unmarshal uses context.getRequiredType().getComponentType())
rejected_leads.reason: Array type resolution is permission-checked as an array (ArrayTypePermission), and array items are independently resolved through mapper.realClass (AbstractCollectionConverter.readItem:73-77), with Array.set rejecting incompatible items. The only un-checked effect is loading the component class; no arbitrary instantiation was demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: JavaClassConverter/JavaMethodConverter/JavaFieldConverter use a private DefaultMapper and resolve arbitrary class names outside the permission chain (XStream.java:941-943, JavaClassConverter.java:74-80)
rejected_leads.reason: Confirmed in source, but the result is inert Class/Method/Field/Constructor values (types are allowed by the default whitelist via Class/Member entries). No XStream code path invokes a Method/Field read from XML, so no concrete impact could be shown in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Unbounded growth of the reference map in AbstractReferenceUnmarshaller (memory-exhaustion DoS)
rejected_leads.reason: The values map is per-unmarshalling and grows linearly with document size; all immutable types are registered non-referenceable (XStream.java:993-1067), so no disproportionate amplification was established. This resembles later, separately reported DoS issues rather than a distinct flaw demonstrable here.

rejected_leads.lead: CachingMapper caches ForbiddenClassException/CannotResolveClassException per element name without bound
rejected_leads.reason: Cache growth is proportional to distinct attacker-supplied names, i.e. bounded by document size; no super-linear amplification or security-control bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in XomDriver/BEAStaxDriver (new XomDriver().createBuilder() returns an unconfigured XOM Builder; StAX drivers only set IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false, never SUPPORT_DTD)
rejected_leads.reason: Real but explicitly documented as a known, accepted limitation in the shipped changes.html (lines 125-129) and faq.html (table at lines 706-732); the default XppDriver does not expand entities. Treated as a documented residual risk rather than this snapshot's unremediated defect.

rejected_leads.lead: DoS/recursion issues in entity expansion or XML nesting depth (possible match for the 1.4.10-era DoS advisory)
rejected_leads.reason: The snapshot contains no depth or entity-expansion limits, but I could not tie any specific code path to a small-input amplification or to a known fixable defect, so no candidate is asserted for this lead.

rejected_leads.lead: XStreamer.is the suspicious API highlighted by the relation index (deserialization hints at XStreamer.java:268/272)
rejected_leads.reason: Kept as the submitted candidate rather than a rejected lead; listed here for traceability of how the index hint was verified against source rather than trusted.

summary: Reviewed the XStream 1.5.0-SNAPSHOT (1.4.10-dev era, ~2017) source snapshot: 477 files under xstream/src/java, xstream-builder, xstream-hibernate, xstream-jmh, xstream-benchmark and the distribution content. The snapshot already contains the 1.4.7-era security framework (com.thoughtworks.xstream.security.*, SecurityMapper) and a default whitelist in XStream.setupSecurity() (XStream.java:633-690), with an allow-list of Null/Primitive/Array/Interface permissions, several type hierarchies (Collection, Map, Number, Throwable, Calendar, TimeZone, Member, Enum, Path) and an explicit type list; AnyTypePermission/ProxyTypePermission are not default. Untrusted XML type resolution flows through SecurityMapper.realClass for element names, `class`/`resolves-to` attributes, aliases and collection items (HierarchicalStreams.readClassType, AbstractCollectionConverter.readItem, AbstractReferenceUnmarshaller), so the classic CVE-2013-7285 gadget path (dynamic proxy + java.beans.EventHandler + ProcessBuilder) is blocked by default and by ReflectionConverter's explicit EventHandler exclusion. I traced the strongest remaining issue to XStreamer.fromXML, which reconstructs an attacker-supplied XStream instance, including its permission list and converter registry, from the same untrusted document and then uses that reconstructed instance to read the payload — a whitelist-bypass design flaw when this public API is used on untrusted input. I also verified the documented-but-unfixed XXE status of XomDriver/BEAStaxDriver (FAQ claims DomDriver/Dom4JDriver/JDom/JDom2 disable DOCTYPE processing — confirmed in code) and rejected several weaker leads (array component types, JavaClassConverter's private DefaultMapper, immutable-reference handling, caching DoS) as not demonstrably exploitable. I did not definitely identify the specific 1.4.10 CVE (CVE-2017-7957-era DoS) in the code; no candidate is asserted for it.
